title: input, forward, output — which chain am I in?
summary: The three chains, what each one actually filters, and why a correct-looking rule does nothing.
analogy: A building with three security desks. The front desk filters people arriving at the building. The inner security desk filters people walking around inside. The desk at the manager's own office filters what leaves the building from there. A rule at the wrong desk checks nothing relevant.

related.label: Worked example of the wrong-chain fault

list: **`input`** — traffic arriving **to the router itself**. Pings to its own address, SSH to the router, DNS to the router.
**`forward`** — traffic **passing through** the router. A client on VLAN 10 reaching the internet, or reaching a server on VLAN 20.
**`output`** — traffic **originating from the router**. Router updates, pings it sends.

p: A rule to stop a client reaching the internet is a **`forward`** rule, not an `input` rule. Putting it in `input` is the single most common RouterOS error, and it fails silently — the rule exists, it just never sees the traffic.
Rule order is evaluated top to bottom and the **first match wins**. An `accept` rule above your `drop` rule makes the drop unreachable.

sections.h: Filtering without NAT is a mistake
p: Forwarded traffic needs **two** things: a filter rule that permits it, and a `srcnat` masquerade rule. Filtering alone allows the request out but the reply cannot come back, because the reply's source address is internal and unroutable.
That presents as `ping: timeout` on an otherwise healthy setup. **Check `/ip/firewall/nat/print` before you start adding filter rules.**
Use `place-before=` to insert rather than append. Appending a drop rule below an existing accept does nothing, and the instinct to "just move things" without checking the counters wastes hours.
sections.code:
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=forward action=accept connection-state=established,related comment="accept established"
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=forward action=drop in-interface=bridge-lan src-address=10.10.30.0/24 out-interface=!bridge-lan place-before=0 comment="guest isolated"
/ip/firewall/filter/print stats

lab.text: Write an accept-established rule at the top of the forward chain.
lab.expect: Return traffic now passes without being re-evaluated against every later rule.

lab.text: Add a guest-isolation rule and confirm it hits.
lab.cmd:
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=forward action=drop src-address=10.10.30.0/24 in-interface=bridge-lan out-interface=!bridge-lan comment="guest isolated"
/ip/firewall/filter/print stats
lab.expect: The packets column goes above zero once a guest tries to reach an internal network.

lab.text: Deliberately put the same rule in `input` and watch it do nothing.
lab.cmd:
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=input action=drop src-address=10.10.30.0/24 comment="wrong chain demo"
/ip/firewall/filter/print stats
lab.expect: Packets stays at 0. The guest is still isolated by the forward rule, so behaviour does not change — the counters tell you why.

lab.text: Remove the demo rule before you forget.

failures.why: Clients get addresses but no internet.
failures.fix: Check `/ip/firewall/nat/print` for a masquerade rule on the WAN interface. Filtering alone drops the replies.

failures.why: A rule appears correct but never matches.
failures.fix: Check the chain and the direction, then `print stats`. Zero packets on a rule you have tested means it is in the wrong place.
`/system/backup/load` from a known-good backup, or connect from the LAN and remove the rule by comment.
